s: Royal reserve of about 28,000 km² north of Riyadh, split by the Ad Dahna dunes
el: About 28,000 km²; 172 plant taxa recorded
te: The desert split by a river of sand
se: A huge royal reserve where the red sands of Ad Dahna run between rawdat meadows, escarpments and gravel plains
sa: محمية ملكية شاسعة تمتدّ فيها رمال الدهناء الحمراء بين الروضات والحافات الصخرية والسهول الحصوية
desc: A royal reserve created by a Royal Order of 2 June 2018 that joined the former At-Tunhat and Al-Khafs reserves and their surroundings, covering about 28,000 km² (2,843,192 ha) north-east of Riyadh, mostly in Riyadh Province with a part in the Eastern Province. A vegetation survey recorded 172 plant taxa in 126 genera and 37 families. Four broad habitats were described: seasonally wet pans, wadis, rawdats and floodplains; escarpments and rocky ridges, which held the highest plant diversity; gravel, sandy or rocky plains and plateaux, with the lowest diversity and cover; and the dunes of the Ad Dahna field, which divides the reserve into northern and southern sections. Protected Planet lists it as WDPA 11956 with 28,340 km².
sig: One of the largest protected areas in central Arabia, conserving rawdat wetlands and dune habitats close to the capital.
ex: Van Rooyen et al. (2026); Saudipedia; Protected Planet
disc: Divided by the Ad Dahna dunes
refs: Van Rooyen, N., Van Rooyen, M., Wolfaard, G., Orban, B., van den Berg, H., Alrefae, A.S., Alowaifeer, A.M. & Gaugris, J. (2026). Analysis of the vegetation in the King Abdulaziz Royal Nature Reserve, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Journal of King Saud University – Science 38, 1682025. https://doi.org/10.25259/JKSUS_168_2025
Saudipedia. King Abdulaziz Royal Reserve. https://saudipedia.com/en/king-abdulaziz-royal-reserve
UNEP-WCMC. King Abdulaziz Royal Reserve (WDPA 11956). Protected Planet. https://www.protectedplanet.net/11956

s: Marine reserve north-west of Jeddah with reefs, mangroves and seagrass
dr: Added to the national reserve list by the Council of Ministers, 2025
te: A sea garden for turtles and dugongs
se: North of Jeddah, Ras Hatiba protects coral reefs, mangroves and seagrass where green turtles, dugongs and dolphins feed
sa: شمال جدة تحمي رأس حاطبة الشعاب المرجانية والقرم والأعشاب البحرية، حيث تتغذّى السلاحف الخضراء والأطوم والدلافين
desc: A marine protected area on the Red Sea coast north-west of Jeddah, covering 5,715 km². It was added to the national list of reserves by Saudi Arabia’s Council of Ministers, backed by biological, natural and social studies from the National Center for Wildlife. The area holds coral reefs, mangroves and seagrass beds and is a key habitat for green turtles, dugongs, whales, dolphins and sharks. It is one of three officially listed protected areas in the Makkah region grouped here, with Majami‘ al-Hadb Reserve and the Haram of Makkah.
sig: Brings a large stretch of central Red Sea reef, mangrove and seagrass habitat under formal protection.
refs: Arab News (12 November 2025). Saudi Arabia protects rare marine ecosystems with 2 new reserves. https://www.arabnews.pk/node/2622363/saudi-arabia
Rosenberg, M.S. Fiddler Crabs: Ras Hatiba, Saudi Arabia (locality record citing Al-Aidaroos 2013 and Eshky et al. 1995). https://fiddlercrab.info/locations/Ras_Hatiba_-_Saudi_Arabia.html
conf: Grouped item SA-A45 (Majami‘ al-Hadb Reserve; Ras Hatiba Reserve; the Haram of Makkah). Only Ras Hatiba had a published coordinate, so the pin marks the Ras Hatiba headland (locality coordinate from fiddlercrab.info), not the whole reserve; Majami‘ al-Hadb (about 2,256.4 km², about 80 km north-east of Ranyah) and the Haram of Makkah are listed but not mapped. Arabic name of Ras Hatiba is a careful transliteration. Designation year 2025 follows the Arab News report of November 2025.

n: Darb Zubaydah – Al-Neqrah and Al-Jafniyah Pool
s: Pilgrim station and pool on the Abbasid Kufa–Makkah road, near ancient copper mines
el: One of 9 Saudi sites on a road of about 1,300 km
te: The pilgrims’ pool by the copper mountain
se: On the old road from Kufa to Makkah, pilgrims rested at An-Neqrah and drew water from the Al-Jafniyah Pool
sa: على الطريق القديم من الكوفة إلى مكة كان الحجاج يستريحون في النقرة ويستقون من بركة الجفنية
desc: A component of the Darb Zubaydah, the pilgrimage road of roughly 1,300 km that linked Kufa with Makkah in the Abbasid period, with stations, water systems and road works. The UNESCO text places Ma‘dan An-Neqrah in a flat agricultural area north of the mountain known as Jabal Ma‘dan. It links the site with ancient copper mining and with pilgrimage facilities, including the Al-Jafniyah Pool. It is one of nine Saudi components of a transnational nomination shared with Iraq.
sig: Shows how the Abbasid pilgrim road used water works and older mining settlements to cross the interior of Arabia.
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2022). The Hajj Pilgrimage Routes: The Darb Zubaydah (Saudi Arabia, Iraq). Tentative List ref. 6577. https://whc.unesco.org/fr/listesindicatives/6577/
conf: Arabic component name is a working transliteration. Region inferred from the coordinates. Timeline is the span of the Abbasid caliphate (AD 750–1258) because the source dates the route only to the Abbasid period.

n: Asiri Highland Landscape: Tihan and Rabea Rufaida
na: المشهد الريفي في مرتفعات عسير: تهان وربع رفيدة
s: Terraced Asir plateau with the Tihan tower and the village of Zabnah
el: Zabnah village lies 12 km north of Borj Tihan
te: Fields stepped across the mountain top
se: In the Asir highlands, low terraces, a watchtower and the old village of Zabnah show how families farmed the mountains
sa: في مرتفعات عسير تروي المدرجات المنخفضة وبرج المراقبة وقرية زبنة القديمة كيف زرع الأهالي الجبال
desc: One of seven elements of the Rural Cultural Landscapes of Sarawat Mountains, a serial nomination in the Makkah, Al-Baha and Asir regions submitted under criteria (ii), (iii) and (v). The fields are low and smoothly terraced and crossed by many wadis. Borj Tihan, in the south of the zone, overlooks the agricultural plateau and the descent to the escarpment. Zabnah, the most significant and best-preserved village, lies 12 km north of the tower and has narrow alleys, gates, an ancient mosque, castles and traditional houses.
sig: Part of a series showing how Sarawat communities shaped the mountains through terracing, water management and vernacular building.
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2023). The Rural Cultural Landscapes of Sarawat Mountains. Tentative List ref. 6640, submitted 23 January 2023. https://whc.unesco.org/fr/listesindicatives/6640/
conf: The source gives no date; the timeline (about the last 500 years) is a broad estimate for the traditional landscape. Arabic name is a working translation; Rabea Rufaida is transliterated as ربع رفيدة.

s: Ancient Fadak, a palm oasis ringed by a lava-stone wall with 18 towers
dr: UNESCO Tentative List 2022 (Ancient Walled Oases of Northern Arabia, ref. 6575)
el: Wall about 6,800 m long and 2 m high
te: The palm oasis inside a black wall
se: Old Fadak hid its springs and 20,000 palms behind a long wall of black volcanic stone
sa: أخفت فدك القديمة عيونها ونخيلها العشرين ألفًا خلف سور طويل من الحجر البركاني الأسود
desc: Al-Ha’it, known in antiquity as Fadak, is a heritage village in Al-Ha’it Governorate about 250 km south-west of Ha’il city. Its history is traced to before 1200 BC, and the Babylonian king Nabonidus conquered it in 553 BC during his stay in Tayma. A defensive wall of volcanic stone about 2 m high and 6,800 m long, with eighteen square towers and several gates, was built in two phases (1834–1847 and after 1909); only its foundation survives. The oasis was known for about twenty thousand palms fed by springs, and the area has rock art, Thamudic inscriptions and a cuneiform inscription of about twenty-six lines.
sig: One of the walled oases of north-west Arabia, a long-lived settlement model in the desert.
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2022). The Ancient Walled Oases of Northern Arabia. Tentative List ref. 6575. https://whc.unesco.org/fr/listesindicatives/6575/
Saudipedia. Al-Ha’it Archaeological Site. https://saudipedia.com/en/al-ha%22it-archaeological-site

Charloux, G. & Alonazi, M. (2025). The Walled Oases Complex in north-west Arabia: evidence for a long-term settlement model in the desert. Antiquity 99(407), e40. https://doi.org/10.15184/aqy.2025.10125
conf: Coordinates are those of the UNESCO Tentative List entry as recorded in the must-have list; the UNESCO page could not be reopened for this record. The app’s hait-pendants record (stone structures, about 2.6 km away) is a different feature. Timeline runs from the earliest date given (before 1200 BC) to the second wall phase (after 1909).

s: Granite domes of Ha’il sheltering the richest wildlife of the arid Arabian interior
dr: UNESCO Tentative List 2023 (Bioclimatic Refugia of Western Arabia, ref. 6638)
el: Two plant taxa found only here
te: The pink mountain island
se: Among pink granite domes near Ha’il, springs and acacia woods keep plants found nowhere else on Earth
sa: بين قباب الجرانيت الوردية قرب حائل تحفظ العيون وغابات السَّمُر نباتات لا توجد في أي مكان آخر على الأرض
desc: A component of the Bioclimatic Refugia of Western Arabia, a natural serial nomination of seven mountain refugia submitted under criteria (vii), (ix) and (x). Jabal Aja is a cluster of pinkish granite domes and pinnacles with ephemeral springs, seeps and Acacia gerrardii woodlands, described as the greatest concentration of biodiversity in the arid interior of the Arabian Peninsula and a Pleistocene refuge. Two taxa are endemic to the site, the grass Trisetaria chaudharyana and the wallflower Erysimum hedgeanum, and relict fauna include griffon vulture, caracal, rock hyrax and Nubian ibex. It is an Important Plant Area and Important Bird Area and lies within the King Salman Royal Nature Reserve.
sig: A biodiversity island in the arid interior that kept cool, moist habitats through dry periods.
disc: Inside King Salman Royal Nature Reserve
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2023). Bioclimatic Refugia of Western Arabia. Tentative List ref. 6638, submitted 23 January 2023. https://whc.unesco.org/fr/listesindicatives/6638/

n: Darb Zubaydah – paved route between Buraykat al-‘Ashshar and Birkat al-‘Ara’ish
na: درب زبيدة – الطريق المرصوف بين بريكة العشار وبركة العرائش
s: About 40 km of Abbasid paving laid across the soft sands of the Nafud
el: Paving about 40 km long and 2–4 m wide
te: A stone road across the dunes
se: To stop camels sinking into Nafud sand, Abbasid builders paved the pilgrim road for about 40 km
sa: كي لا تغوص الإبل في رمال النفود رصف البنّاؤون العباسيون طريق الحجاج نحو 40 كيلومترًا
desc: A stretch of the Darb Zubaydah, the Abbasid pilgrimage road of roughly 1,300 km between Kufa and Makkah. The UNESCO text notes that the soft sand of the Nefud desert was a significant obstacle that made paving necessary. Surveyed pavements cross the dunes for about 40 km and are two to four metres wide. It is one of nine Saudi components of a transnational nomination shared with Iraq.
sig: Rare engineering evidence of how the pilgrim road was built to cross a sand sea.
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2022). The Hajj Pilgrimage Routes: The Darb Zubaydah (Saudi Arabia, Iraq). Tentative List ref. 6577. https://whc.unesco.org/fr/listesindicatives/6577/
conf: Arabic component name is a working transliteration. Region inferred from the coordinates. Timeline is the span of the Abbasid caliphate (AD 750–1258) because the source dates the route only to the Abbasid period.

n: Wadi Lajb and Jabal al-Qahar bioclimatic refugium
s: Jazan canyon with Arabia’s finest valley forest, cloud forest and endemic fish
dr: UNESCO Tentative List 2023 (Bioclimatic Refugia of Western Arabia, ref. 6638)
el: Al-Jabal al-Aswad rises to 2,497 m
te: The green canyon of Jazan
se: A deep canyon with a stream that never dries, full of fig trees, rare fish and cloud forest above
sa: وادٍ عميق يجري فيه جدول لا يجفّ، تملؤه أشجار التين والأسماك النادرة وتعلوه غابة سحابية
desc: A component of the Bioclimatic Refugia of Western Arabia, on a sandstone-capped massif that receives high orographic rain in spring and late summer and winter mists. Wadi Lajb is a deep canyon with the Kingdom’s most important patches of Arabian valley forest and a perennial stream with endemic freshwater fish such as Garra sahilia and Garra tibanica. Al-Jabal al-Aswad in the south-east reaches 2,497 m and carries a cloud forest of African juniper (Juniperus procera), while dense dawm palm woodlands grow on a granite pluton in the south-west. Site endemics include Peucedanum inaccessum, Huernia laevis and Aloe × qaharensis; it is an Important Bird Area.
sig: A refuge for Afrotropical relict plants and Arabian endemic fish, birds and reptiles in the far south-west.
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2023). Bioclimatic Refugia of Western Arabia. Tentative List ref. 6638, submitted 23 January 2023. https://whc.unesco.org/fr/listesindicatives/6638/
UNEP-WCMC. Wadi Lajb / Jabal al-Qahar (WDPA 555624834). Protected Planet. https://www.protectedplanet.net/555624834
conf: Timeline starts at the 2023 Tentative List submission

s: Ancient basalt dam about 30 m high across a valley of Harrat Khaybar
el: About 30 m high; about 135 m survives
te: The black wall that held back floods
se: South of Khaybar, a giant wall of black basalt once blocked a deep valley to store rare rain
sa: جنوب خيبر سدّ جدار عملاق من البازلت الأسود واديًا عميقًا ليخزّن ماء المطر النادر
desc: One of five dams in the serial Tentative List entry Water Management in Saudi Arabia: The Ancient Dams. Also called Sadd Qusaybah or the Khaybar Dam, it lies about 30 km south of the Khaybar oasis in Harrat Khaybar. Built of black basalt, it is about 30 m high and once spanned about 200 m of a deep, steep valley; about 135 m survive after almost a third was breached. The upstream face carries a yellow mortar plaster for waterproofing, and a double flight of steps descends the downstream side.
sig: A monumental example of ancient water storage in the lava fields of north-west Arabia.
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2023). Water Management in Saudi Arabia: The Ancient Dams. Tentative List ref. 6637. https://whc.unesco.org/fr/listesindicatives/6637/

Madain Project. Sadd al-Bint (Khaybar Dam). https://madainproject.com/sadd_al_bint_(khaybar_dam)
conf: The UNESCO page could not be opened; coordinates are from the blog mirror of its component table. The dam is described only as pre-Islamic or Early Islamic, so the timeline (about AD 250–700) is a broad estimate. Region inferred from the coordinates.

s: Red granite crags near Yanbu with junipers, dragon trees and Nubian ibex
dr: UNESCO Tentative List 2023 (Bioclimatic Refugia of Western Arabia, ref. 6638)
el: One plant taxon known only from here
te: The mountain of dragon trees
se: High on the red crags of Jabal Radwa grow junipers, aloes and ancient dragon trees where ibex climb
sa: على صخور جبل رضوى الحمراء تنمو أشجار العرعر والصبر ودم الأخوين القديمة حيث تتسلّق الوعول
desc: A component of the Bioclimatic Refugia of Western Arabia, formed of reddish granite crags and pinnacles with Phoenician juniper woodlands, dragon trees, aloes and plants of Mediterranean origin. A Pterocephalus species new to science (aff. sanctus) is endemic to the site, and Arabian endemics include Acacia johnwoodii, Aloe porphyrostachys and Teucrium hijazicum. Relict taxa include the Nubian dragon tree (Dracaena ombet) and Origanum syriacum, and the mountain hosts Nubian ibex, idmi gazelle and possibly the Arabian leopard. Its northern and western parts fall within the Red Sea Project area.
sig: A Hijaz mountain refuge where Mediterranean and African plant lineages survive side by side.
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2023). Bioclimatic Refugia of Western Arabia. Tentative List ref. 6638, submitted 23 January 2023. https://whc.unesco.org/fr/listesindicatives/6638/
UNEP-WCMC. Jabal Radwa (WDPA 555624829). Protected Planet. https://www.protectedplanet.net/555624829
conf: Timeline starts at the 2023 Tentative List submission

n: Egyptian Hajj Road – Al-Swaiq site, Yanbu
na: طريق الحج المصري – موقع السويق في ينبع
s: Coastal station at Yanbu on the pilgrim road from Egypt to Makkah
dr: UNESCO Tentative List 2015 (Egyptian Hajj Road, ref. 6028)
el: One of 16 Saudi components of the road
te: A stop for pilgrims from Africa
se: Pilgrims from Egypt, North Africa and Andalusia passed Yanbu on the long coastal road to Makkah
sa: مرّ حجاج مصر والمغرب والأندلس بينبع على الطريق الساحلي الطويل إلى مكة
desc: A component of the Egyptian Hajj Road, which linked Egypt with Makkah and Madinah and was used by pilgrims from Egypt, Sudan, Central Africa, Morocco, Andalusia and Sicily. The road began at Haqel on the Gulf of Aqaba and split into an inland trail towards Madinah and a coastal trail through stations such as Al-Muwailih, Dhuba, Al-Wajh and Yanbu to Al-Juhfa and Makkah. The route had wells, forts, markets and inscriptions and declined as sea travel replaced it, especially after the Suez Canal opened. The UNESCO entry lists Al-Swaiq at Yanbu among its 16 components but gives no separate description.
sig: Marks the Yanbu station of one of the great historic pilgrimage routes to Makkah.
disc: Yanbu station on the coastal trail
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2015). Egyptian Hajj Road. Tentative List ref. 6028, submitted 8 April 2015. https://whc.unesco.org/fr/listesindicatives/6028/
conf: Coordinates converted from the UTM values (zone 37R) in the UNESCO entry. The source gives no date for this site; the timeline (7th century to 1884, when the overland route ended) is a broad estimate. Arabic name is a working translation.

n: Prehistoric stone structures of Harrat Khaybar
s: Lava plateau with hundreds of desert kites, wheels, pendants and mustatils
dr: UNESCO Tentative List 2023 (Prehistoric Stone Structures, ref. 6636)
el: 917 kites counted in a 2014 survey
te: Stone shapes drawn on black lava
ta: أشكال من الحجر مرسومة على الحمم السوداء
se: Across the black lava of Khaybar, ancient people built giant stone traps, wheels and long rectangles seen best from the sky
sa: على حمم خيبر السوداء بنى القدماء مصائد حجرية عملاقة ودوائر ومستطيلات طويلة لا تُرى كاملةً إلا من السماء
desc: A component of Prehistoric Stone Structures in Saudi Arabia, a serial nomination of 10 components for which a preliminary estimate gives about 1 million stone structures. Harrat Khaybar is a lava plateau of about 12,000 km² with desert kites of various shapes, wheels, cairns, pendants and mustatils, notably near Samhah. Density is highest near the oases of Khaybar and Al-Ha’it, and a 2014 survey identified 917 kites; barbed kites are exclusive to Khaybar. The plateau, with its volcanoes and lava caves, is also being proposed as a UNESCO Global Geopark.
sig: One of the densest landscapes of prehistoric stone architecture in Arabia.
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2023). Prehistoric Stone Structures in Saudi Arabia. Tentative List ref. 6636, submitted 23 January 2023. https://whc.unesco.org/fr/listesindicatives/6636

World Heritage Tentative List (blog mirror of the UNESCO text). Saudi Arabia – Prehistoric Stone Structures in Saudi Arabia (component coordinates). https://worldheritagetentativelist.blogspot.com/2021/03/saudi-arabia-prehistoric-stone.html
conf: Coordinates are the component point from the blog mirror of the UNESCO table. Not dated in the source; the timeline is a broad estimate for prehistoric stone structures in Arabia. No app point lies within a few km (al-natah-khaybar and the mustatils are about 40 km north).

n: Syrian Hajj Road – Al-Buraika fort and pool
na: طريق الحج الشامي – قلعة البريكة وبركتها
s: Fort and water pool on the pilgrim road from Damascus to Madinah
dr: UNESCO Tentative List 2015 (Syrian Hajj Road, ref. 6027)
el: One of 11 Saudi components of a 1,307 km road
te: A fort guarding the pilgrims’ water
se: Between Tabuk and AlUla, pilgrims from Damascus stopped at Al-Buraika for water and safety
sa: بين تبوك والعلا كان حجاج الشام يتوقفون عند البريكة طلبًا للماء والأمان
desc: A component of the Syrian Hajj Road, a route of about 1,307 km from Damascus to Madinah known in early Islamic times as the Attabukiyah road. Stations included That Al-Hajj, Tabuk, Al-Akhdhar, Al-Mu’azam, Al-Hijr and Al-Ula, with pools, tanks, canals, forts, mosques, bridges and markets along the way. Forts on the route stored food for the return journey and sheltered the poor, the lost and those left behind through illness or injury. The UNESCO entry lists Al-Buraika fort and pool among its 11 components without a separate description.
sig: One of the fortified water stations that made the long desert crossing from Damascus possible.
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2015). Syrian Hajj Road. Tentative List ref. 6027, submitted 8 April 2015. https://whc.unesco.org/fr/listesindicatives/6027/
conf: Coordinates converted from the UTM values (zone 37R) in the UNESCO entry. The source gives no date for this fort; the timeline (7th to early 20th century) is a broad estimate for the route’s use. Region (Madinah) not confirmed; the point lies between Al-Mu’azam and Al-Hijr. Arabic name is a working translation.

s: Stone dam 212 m long in Wadi Thumalah south-west of Taif
el: 212 m long and 25 m high
te: The great stone dam of Taif
se: Between two mountains near Taif, a stone dam 212 metres long has stood across the valley for some 1,300 years
sa: بين جبلين قرب الطائف يقف سدّ حجري طوله 212 مترًا عبر الوادي منذ نحو 1300 عام
desc: One of five dams in the Tentative List entry Water Management in Saudi Arabia: The Ancient Dams. The dam lies between two mountains in Wadi Thumalah, about 30 km south-west of Taif. It is 212 m long, 25 m high and 10 m wide at the top, built of massive stones with rubble packed between two walls, larger stones on the back face and a mortar coating on the facade and upper parts. A partly illegible inscription beside the dam suggests it was built in the reign of Mu‘awiya ibn Abi Sufyan; it is also known as Thumalah Dam and Bani Hilal Dam.
sig: A large, well-preserved Early Islamic dam showing water engineering in the Hijaz highlands.
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2023). Water Management in Saudi Arabia: The Ancient Dams. Tentative List ref. 6637. https://whc.unesco.org/fr/listesindicatives/6637/

Saudipedia. Al-Samallagi Ancient Dam. https://saudipedia.com/en/article/3644/history/landmarks-and-monuments/al-samallagi-ancient-dam

n: Jabal Batharah and Wadi Turabah bioclimatic refugium
s: Granite spires and a perennial stream over 20 km long with three endemic fish
dr: UNESCO Tentative List 2023 (Bioclimatic Refugia of Western Arabia, ref. 6638)
el: Perennial stream flowing more than 20 km
te: The mountain stream that never stops
se: Below grey granite spires, the Wadi Turabah stream flows all year, home to fish and frogs found only in Arabia
sa: تحت قمم الجرانيت الرمادية يجري جدول وادي تربة طوال العام، موطنًا لأسماك وضفادع لا توجد إلا في الجزيرة العربية
desc: A component of the Bioclimatic Refugia of Western Arabia, with grey granite spires, domes and buttresses, montane meadows, tree heather thickets and woodlands of African juniper, wild olive and Acacia origena. On the east side the perennial Wadi Turabah stream flows for more than 20 km through parallel metamorphic ridges and valleys. It is described as one of the richest streams in the Kingdom, with three endemic freshwater fish (Carasobarbus apoensis, Cyprinion mhalensis and Garra buettikeri) and endemic and relict frogs and toads. The site is an Important Bird Area, with species such as Philby’s partridge and the buff-breasted wheatear.
sig: A rare combination of montane woodland and a permanent stream in western Arabia’s mountains.
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2023). Bioclimatic Refugia of Western Arabia. Tentative List ref. 6638, submitted 23 January 2023. https://whc.unesco.org/fr/listesindicatives/6638/
UNEP-WCMC. Jabal Batharah / Wadi Turabah (WDPA 11974). Protected Planet. https://www.protectedplanet.net/11974
conf: Timeline starts at the 2023 Tentative List submission. Arabic spelling of Batharah (بثرة) is a careful transliteration.

s: Pilgrim station with two near-perfect reservoirs fed by an aqueduct
el: Two large reservoirs in almost perfect condition
te: Water tanks for the last miles to Makkah
ta: خزانات الماء للأميال الأخيرة إلى مكة
se: Near the end of the road to Makkah, two great tanks still hold the shape builders gave them centuries ago
sa: قرب نهاية الطريق إلى مكة ما زال خزانان كبيران يحتفظان بالشكل الذي بناهما عليه البنّاؤون قبل قرون
desc: A station on the Darb Zubaydah, the Abbasid pilgrimage road of roughly 1,300 km between Kufa and Makkah. The site has two large reservoirs in almost perfect condition: a rectangular catchment tank and a larger circular tank. An aqueduct brought water to them from Wadi al-Aqiq. It is one of nine Saudi components of a transnational nomination shared with Iraq.
sig: Among the best-preserved water installations of the Abbasid pilgrim road.
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2022). The Hajj Pilgrimage Routes: The Darb Zubaydah (Saudi Arabia, Iraq). Tentative List ref. 6577. https://whc.unesco.org/fr/listesindicatives/6577/

s: Tower at Rabigh, close to Al-Juhfa, the miqat of Egyptian pilgrims
dr: UNESCO Tentative List 2015 (Egyptian Hajj Road, ref. 6028)
el: One of 16 Saudi components of the road
te: The tower near the pilgrims’ gateway
se: At Rabigh, near the place where Egyptian pilgrims put on their ihram, a tower marks the old coastal road
sa: في رابغ، قرب المكان الذي كان حجاج مصر يُحرمون منه، يدلّ برج على الطريق الساحلي القديم
desc: A component of the Egyptian Hajj Road, which linked Egypt with Makkah and Madinah for pilgrims from Egypt, Sudan, Central Africa, Morocco, Andalusia and Sicily. The coastal trail ran from Haqel on the Gulf of Aqaba through stations such as Al-Muwailih, Dhuba, Al-Wajh and Yanbu to Al-Juhfa and Makkah. Historical accounts cited in the nomination note that Rabigh lies close to Al-Juhfa, the miqat where Egyptian pilgrims entered ihram. The UNESCO entry lists Rabigh Tower among its 16 components but gives no separate description of the tower.
sig: Marks the approach to Al-Juhfa on the historic Egyptian pilgrimage road.
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2015). Egyptian Hajj Road. Tentative List ref. 6028, submitted 8 April 2015. https://whc.unesco.org/fr/listesindicatives/6028/

sa: على مدى 50 عامًا حوّلت هذه المصفاة في جدة النفط الخام إلى وقود لغرب المملكة
desc: One of five components of the Tentative List entry The Oil Industrial Heritage in Saudi Arabia, with Dammam Well No. 7, the Trans-Arabian Pipeline, King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals and Dhahran Camp. The refinery started operations in 1967 and had a production capacity of 80,000 barrels per day, 2.7 percent of the Kingdom’s refining capacity. In November 2017 Saudi Aramco shut it down and converted the complex into a distribution hub.
sig: The Red Sea coast’s link in the story of how oil reshaped modern Saudi Arabia.

s: Stone apiary for about 1,300 hives on curved terraces south of Taif
el: Room for about 1,300 beehives
te: A stone tower block for bees
se: Near Taif, families built a stone apiary for some 1,300 hives, stacked like floors of a tall building
sa: قرب الطائف بنت الأسر منحلًا حجريًا يتّسع لنحو 1300 خلية، مصفوفة كطوابق مبنى شاهق
desc: The first element of the Rural Cultural Landscapes of Sarawat Mountains, at the abandoned village of Kherfi in the governorate of Maysan, south of Taif. The apiaries are probably about 500 years old and were passed down within one family; the ensemble could hold 1,300 beehives on different levels. Built of solid stone with stone columns supporting the upper floors, the hives line curved terraces cut into a steep mountainside, terraces made for beekeeping as well as farming. A 20 m high stone fortress overlooks the apiaries, and the site also has agricultural terraces, livestock areas and village ruins.
sig: An exceptional surviving monument of traditional mountain beekeeping in the Sarawat.
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2023). The Rural Cultural Landscapes of Sarawat Mountains. Tentative List ref. 6640, submitted 23 January 2023. https://whc.unesco.org/fr/listesindicatives/6640/
conf: Timeline uses the source’s ‘probably 500 years old’. Arabic name is a working translation; Kherfi is transliterated as الخرفي.

s: Well-preserved circular pilgrim reservoir 32 m across
el: Circular basin 32 m in diameter
te: A round pool for thirsty caravans
se: In the far north, pilgrims walked down stone steps into a round reservoir 32 metres wide
sa: في أقصى الشمال كان الحجاج ينزلون درجات حجرية إلى خزان مستدير عرضه 32 مترًا
desc: The first Saudi station listed for the Darb Zubaydah, the Abbasid pilgrimage road of roughly 1,300 km between Kufa and Makkah. The site has a very well-preserved circular basin notable for its size, with a diameter of 32 m. It has a two-layer wall and a staircase giving access to the water. It is one of nine Saudi components of a transnational nomination shared with Iraq.
sig: A clear example of the large water basins that sustained pilgrims on the Abbasid road.

s: More than 1,500 stone circles and cruciform ‘wheel’ tombs at the edge of the Empty Quarter
dr: UNESCO Tentative List 2023 (Prehistoric Stone Structures, ref. 6636)
el: More than 1,500 circular structures in about 4 km²
te: Stone wheels beneath the cliffs
se: Where Wadi Ad-Dawasir meets the Tuwaiq cliffs, ancient people built hundreds of stone circles and wheel-shaped tombs
sa: حيث يلتقي وادي الدواسر بجروف طويق بنى القدماء مئات الدوائر الحجرية والمدافن على هيئة عجلات
desc: A component of Prehistoric Stone Structures in Saudi Arabia, at the north-western fringe of the Empty Quarter where Wadi Ad-Dawasir meets the Tuwaiq escarpment. Structures lie at the foot of the cliffs and on the plateau above. More than 1,500 circular stone structures occur in the wadi, notably cruciform tombs (‘wheels’) of 25 m diameter, concentrated in a sector of about 4 km². The serial nomination covers 10 components and a preliminary estimate of about 1 million stone structures across Saudi Arabia.
sig: A dense prehistoric funerary landscape at the meeting of the Tuwaiq escarpment and the Empty Quarter.

s: About 80 rock-cut tombs of Midian on the Egyptian Hajj Road
dr: UNESCO Tentative List 2015 (Egyptian Hajj Road, ref. 6028)
el: About 80 tombs in 12 rock outcrops
te: The carved caves of Midian
se: At Al-Bad’, tomb fronts carved into sandstone cliffs mark ancient Midian, a water stop for pilgrims
sa: في البدع تدلّ واجهات المقابر المنحوتة في جروف الحجر الرملي على مدين القديمة، محطة ماء للحجاج
desc: Magha’ir Shu’ayb in Al-Bad’ Governorate, Tabuk Province, about 225 km from Tabuk city, is the first listed component of the Egyptian Hajj Road. It has around eighty tombs spread over twelve rock outcrops, arranged in four neighbouring groups forming a semicircle, with carved facades in sandstone and limestone, some bearing triangles, crowns and overlapping arches. The site was used for burial and housing by the Nabataeans and earlier by the Midianites, and the region’s prosperity is dated to 100 BC–AD 550. The UNESCO text links the place with the Prophet Shu’ayb and describes it as a pilgrim stop with water and pools.
sig: A landmark of ancient Midian that remained a water station on the pilgrimage road from Egypt.
disc: Water stop on the Egyptian Hajj Road

n: Syrian Hajj Road – That Hajj (Dhat al-Hajj) Fort
na: طريق الحج الشامي – قلعة ذات الحاج
s: Ottoman pilgrim fort of 1559, the first Saudi station on the road from Damascus
dr: Built 1559; UNESCO Tentative List 2015 (Syrian Hajj Road, ref. 6027)
el: Fort built in 1559
te: The fort at the pilgrims’ well
se: North of Tabuk, an Ottoman fort built in 1559 guarded the water that pilgrims from Damascus needed
sa: شمال تبوك حرست قلعة عثمانية بُنيت سنة 1559 الماء الذي احتاجه حجاج الشام
desc: The first listed component of the Syrian Hajj Road, a route of about 1,307 km from Damascus to Madinah. That El-Hajj was a station between Halat Ammar and Tabuk. An Ottoman fortress was built here in 1559, following earlier forts on the route, and all such forts stood within musket-shot of a water reservoir. Forts on the road stored food for the return journey and sheltered the poor, the lost and pilgrims left behind through illness or injury.
sig: An early Ottoman fort marking the entry of the Damascus pilgrim road into present-day Saudi Arabia.
disc: Station between Halat Ammar and Tabuk

se: At the northern tip of Al-Ahsa, an old village and its palm grove show how oasis life once looked

desc: Component 1563-010 of the Al-Ahsa Oasis, an Evolving Cultural Landscape, inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2018. It covers 63.35 ha, with a buffer zone of 191 ha, and is the most northerly part of the property. It includes a traditional village and a palm grove; the ICOMOS evaluation described the village as mostly deserted and largely ruinous. The whole oasis has more than 2.5 million palm trees.
sig: Preserves the traditional village form at the northern edge of one of the world’s largest palm oases.

It is a drainage zone of 2,170 ha that collects water flowing out of the oasis, with a buffer zone of 10,780 ha. The ICOMOS evaluation notes that it includes a mangrove area. It is the largest single component of the serial property after the Eastern Oasis.

s: Rocky ridge covered with 245 petroglyphs and 438 inscriptions, once a caravan toll station
el: 245 petroglyphs and 438 inscriptions
te: The rock where caravans paid their toll
ta: الصخرة التي دفعت عندها القوافل رسومها
se: On a ridge of giant boulders near Najran, travellers carved hundreds of pictures and messages over thousands of years
sa: على مرتفع من الصخور الضخمة قرب نجران حفر المسافرون مئات الصور والرسائل عبر آلاف السنين
desc: Component 1619bis-003 of the Ḥimā Cultural Area, a World Heritage property inscribed in 2021 under criterion (iii), covering 3.66 ha. It is a low rocky ridge with very large angular boulders and a vertical cliff, densely covered with 245 petroglyphs and 438 inscriptions; one inscription is estimated at about 1,300 to 1,350 years old from micro-erosion calibration. The site holds the most recent scientific evidence of surface water in the area, which helps estimate when the aquifer lowered and the region became desert, and a caravan toll station once stood here. Across the property, petroglyphs span at least 7,000 years.
sig: A dense record of travellers’ art and writing, and evidence for the drying of the Najran landscape.

s: Meandering cliff on Wadi Saad with thousands of petroglyphs and polished rock slides
el: 112 ha; thousands of petroglyphs
te: The cliff of cattle and dancers
se: Along a winding cliff near Najran, thousands of carvings show cattle and people, beside a dry rock waterfall
sa: على جرف متعرّج قرب نجران تصوّر آلاف النقوش أبقارًا وبشرًا، بجوار شلال صخري جاف
desc: Component 1619bis-006 of the Ḥimā Cultural Area, a World Heritage property inscribed in 2021, covering 112 ha. It lies immediately north of and along Wadi Saad at the base of a meandering cliff, with thousands of petroglyphs on the cliff and on large sandstone blocks at its foot. Four polished ‘slides’ lie on a sloping panel in front of a ‘waterfall’ feature, and panels east of the waterfall show bovids and human figures, sometimes interacting. ICOMOS recommended Heritage Impact Assessments before any tourism project here.
sig: One of the richest rock-art panels of the Ḥimā property, rich in scenes of people and cattle.
